The traffic light reflects the static readiness signals by default; a script in code_error that stopped with an error makes it red, as a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure, and a script in one of the other three groups keeps it from being green. Calls that need a screen, which the run does not have (dev.print(), dev.copy2pdf(), dev.copy2eps(), savePlot(), windows(), win.graph(), x11(), quartz(), View()), are replaced before the run by calls that need none, which modifications records as screen_call_replaced. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Food insecurity (FI) is associated with obesity and poor physical and mental health, but whether it causes these outcomes is unknown. In Part A, we developed a protocol that manipulates two characteristics of eating patterns associated with FI, irregularity and uncertainty, and piloted it in 12 healthy, food-secure women to establish its feasibility, acceptability and fidelity. In a mixed 2 × 2 cross-over design, participants completed two 2week interventions with regular or irregular meal schedules and were either informed of or uncertain about their schedule in advance. The protocol was feasible and acceptable: retention was 86% and engagement with momentary assessment met our preregistered 80% threshold. Dietary recalls confirmed that the irregularity manipulation altered eating patterns, and post-intervention questionnaires confirmed that the uncertainty manipulation increased worry about meal timing. In Part B, we compared outcomes before and after each intervention. None of our preregistered predictions was supported: irregular meals did not reduce diet-induced thermogenesis (DIT), uncertainty did not amplify any effect of irregularity and uncertainty did not increase anxiety or depression symptoms. However, equivalence tests could not exclude meaningful effects. Exploratory analyses, including a pooled analysis of the three preregistered outcomes, suggested that, rather than uncertainty amplifying the effects of irregularity, any departure from a regular meal schedule known in advance may be sufficient to shift health-relevant outcomes including DIT, food intake and affective state. With modifications, this protocol could be used in adequately powered trials to test whether meal irregularity and uncertainty contribute to the health effects of FI.

1. Introduction

Food insecurity (FI), defined as limited and uncertain access to nutritionally adequate food, has a constellation of adverse correlates, including increased odds of obesity, reduced physical and mental health and increased all-cause mortality (Arenas et al., 2019; Gundersen et al., 2018; Gundersen & Seligman, 2017; Nettle et al., 2017; Nettle & Bateson, 2026). It is currently unclear whether FI directly causes these outcomes and the nature of the mechanisms involved (Bateson & Pepper, 2023; Nettle & Bateson, 2026). Moreover, because FI is measured with questionnaires that probe multiple components of psychological hardships and nutritional deprivation, it is also unclear which components of FI contribute to these effects. To address these knowledge gaps, experimental studies are needed to establish whether specific features of eating patterns associated with FI influence outcome variables related to energy balance, body weight and health. The current study develops a protocol for manipulating two such features that we hypothesise are important, namely the irregularity and uncertainty of meals.

In this paper, 'meal' is used to describe a discrete eating occasion, during which any quantity of food or drink other than water is consumed; no distinction is drawn between meals and snacks. 'Irregularity' refers to variability between days in the number and timing of meals. In contrast, 'uncertainty' is used to describe the cognitive state arising from a lack of advance knowledge about the timing of future meals. Irregularity is thus a property of the pattern of meals and can be quantified from a record of when meals occur; uncertainty is a state of the person and must be inferred or self-reported. The two can be dissociated in principle-a missed meal may be anticipated as readily as unanticipated, and a regular schedule may be unknown to the person following it-but they are likely to co-occur under conditions of FI. For example, someone who depends on the unpredictable availability of free food obtained via a food-sharing app is likely to have both more irregular meals and greater uncertainty about when they will eat.

Evidence from analysis of 24-hour dietary recalls collected in the USA and UK shows that the largest effect of FI on diet is more irregular patterns of eating (Nettle & Bateson, 2019; Shinwell et al., 2021): FI is associated with higher variance in the intervals between meals, higher variance in the time of the first meal each day and higher variance in the number of daily meals. Supporting the notion that irregular eating may promote weight gain and compromise metabolic health, variance in the intervals between meals partially mediates the positive association between FI and body mass index (BMI) (Nettle & Bateson, 2019). Although there are associations between FI and diet quality (people with FI eat fewer different foods and relatively less fibre, less protein and more carbohydrate), there is no association between FI and total energy intake, suggesting that the mechanism linking FI to higher body weight may not be greater energy intake (Nettle & Bateson, 2019; Shinwell et al., 2021).

Evidence that irregular meals could trigger weight gain in the absence of increased intake comes from randomised controlled trials in free-living women showing that irregular meal timing causes a reduction in diet-induced thermogenesis (DIT; Alhussain et al., 2016 Alhussain et al., , 2022;; Farshchi et al., 2004 Farshchi et al., , 2005)). In these trials (henceforth the 'Nottingham protocol'), variability in the number of meals per day was manipulated for a 2-week period. A regular condition (6 meals per day) was compared with an irregular condition (3-9 meals per day) in a counterbalanced, cross-over design. In the two latest studies using this protocol, diet quality and mean daily energy intake were held constant between conditions, ensuring that meal regularity was the only difference (Alhussain et al., 2016 (Alhussain et al., , 2022)).

The authors drew no connection between their manipulation and FI. However, the Nottingham protocol produced a pattern of eating similar in some respects to that described in people living with FI, including higher variance in both the intervals between meals and the number of daily meals. The results from these trials therefore suggest that the increased irregularity in meal timing seen in food-insecure participants could be sufficient to trigger the energy saving necessary to fuel increased adipogenesis in the absence of increased energy intake. The Nottingham studies did not find any evidence for an effect of irregular meals on body weight, but this is unsurprising following a 2-week intervention. Under reasonable assumptions for how a difference in DIT measured over 3 hours would scale to energy expenditure over 24 hours and applying the Hall et al. (2011) dynamic model to estimate the effects on weight gain over two weeks, we estimate that the decrease in DIT caused by irregular meals reported in the Nottingham studies would translate into a weight difference after 14 days of only between 24 and 87 g, depending on the trial (unpublished calculations).

To our knowledge, no published human study has manipulated the uncertainty of meals and measured effects on body weight or any component of energy balance. In the Nottingham protocol, participants were told their eating schedule in both conditions, so should not have been uncertain about the timing of their meals in either condition. Experiments on animal models provide proof that irregular and uncertain access to food causes increased fat storage independent of energy intake or diet quality (Andrews et al., 2021; Bateson et al., 2021; Gil, Lund, Żylicz, Ranea-Robles, et al., 2025), suggesting that fat storage must be driven by a shift in fuel partitioning financed by reduced energy expenditure (Friedman et al., 2024). Animal experiments typically confound irregularity with uncertainty, because manipulating uncertainty while holding irregularity constant is methodologically challenging (van Berkel et al., 2018). One recent exception compared birds that differed only in their ability to anticipate irregular periods of food deprivation, and found poorer regulation of body weight when food deprivation was unpredictable (Parker et al., 2025). In birds at least, uncertainty about access to food therefore has consequences for body weight regulation over and above effects of irregularity.

Uncertainty in general is hypothesised to be central to understanding the negative health impacts of stress (Morriss et al., 2022; Peters et al., 2017; Weaver et al., 2021). In the context of eating behaviour, uncertainty arising from lack of perceived control is a key difference separating FI, which is associated with poor health, from voluntary intermittent fasting, which is associated with improved health. Thus, despite the current lack of evidence in humans, uncertainty about future access to food is likely to contribute to the health impacts of FI. We hypothesise that irregular and uncertain food consumption are causal factors contributing to the higher body weight and adverse physical and mental health outcomes associated with FI. Furthermore, we hypothesise that the effect of irregularity will be amplified by the uncertainty about future food consumption.

The study had two aims. Part A concerned the development of a novel experimental protocol, with the following objectives. (1) To develop a protocol that manipulates irregularity and uncertainty of meals, and to pilot this protocol in free-living, healthy, adult women to establish feasibility, acceptability and participant compliance. (2) To verify that the protocol manipulated what it was designed to manipulate, namely the pattern of eating and participants' advance knowledge of their meal schedule. Part B used the pilot to estimate the effects of the intervention on outcome variables, with the following objectives. (3) To replicate the finding from the Nottingham studies that two weeks of exposure to irregular meals causes reduced DIT. (4) To test the hypothesis that the latter effect is amplified by adding uncertainty about the timing of meals. (5) To test the hypothesis that uncertainty about the timing of meals would cause increased symptoms of anxiety and depression, over and above those arising from meal irregularity alone. (6) To additionally explore effects on body weight, appetite, energy intake, macronutrient intake, resting metabolic rate, substrate oxidation, additional measures of mood and motivation to rest and move.

2. Methods

>Methods

2.1. Preregistration and ethics

The study design, predictions and analysis plan were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/6PTFY). The Newcastle University Faculty of Medical Science Research Ethics Committee (ref. 2403_2/24488) granted ethical approval for the study. Informed consent was obtained from all participants.

2.2.

Participants

Participants were an opportunity sample of staff and students at Newcastle University recruited via word of mouth, a poster and advertisements on an internal social networking site. Healthy women (assigned female sex at birth, currently identifying as a woman) aged 18-45 years with a BMI of 18-25 kg•m -² were recruited. Exclusion criteria included: food insecurity (USDA 6-item screener ≥2); current medication use (except oral contraceptives); ongoing medical investigation or treatment for a condition that could affect study outcomes; pregnancy or lactation; current smoking; history of kidney, liver, or cardiovascular disease; diabetes; gastrointestinal disorder; cancer within the past year; current dieting or weight-loss attempts; current or historical eating disorder; moderate-to-severe anxiety or depression (GAD-7 or PHQ-9 ≥10); night-shift work; food allergies; and participation in another conflicting research study. Participants were compensated with a £200 gift voucher on completion of the study.

2.3.

Study design

We designed a novel dietary intervention to manipulate irregularity (two levels: Regular versus Irregular) and uncertainty (two levels: Informed versus Uncertain) of meals (Figure 1A) in free-living participants.

The experiment had a mixed, 2 x 2 factorial design. As in the Nottingham protocol, all participants completed both the Regular and Irregular conditions in a counterbalanced, crossover design, with a two-week wash-out between the two intervention periods. We added a manipulation of uncertainty whereby half of the participants were allocated to an Informed condition and half to an Uncertain condition. Thus, the comparison of Regular versus Irregular was within participants and the comparison of Informed versus Uncertain was between participants. This factorial design allows testing of the effects of irregularity and uncertainty as main effects and in interaction.

On recruitment, each participant was randomly assigned to one of the four groups shown in Figure 1A. Participants were not told the specific hypotheses under test. All data were recorded by visit number and the key linking a participant's ID to the conditions they received at each visit was kept separately to reduce the likelihood of experimenter bias. All data cleaning and processing prior to conducting the inferential statistics was conducted blind to condition.

2.4.

Sample size

We aimed for a total of 12 participants (3 in each of the 4 groups). This yielded n = 12 for testing the within-subjects effect of Regularity versus Irregularity and n = 6 per condition for testing the between-subjects effect of Informed versus Uncertain. The experiment was powered to replicate the within-subject effect of irregular food consumption on DIT (the four studies using the Nottingham protocol had sample sizes of 9-11 participants and all reported significant effects of irregularity on DIT). It was likely to be underpowered to test the effect of uncertainty, but our objective for the uncertainty manipulation was to establish its feasibility (Part A) rather than to provide a strong test of its effects (Part B). 2.5.

Manipulated variables: meal irregularity and uncertainty

We manipulated the eating schedules of free-living participants by asking them to eat at prescribed times each day for two weeks. Participants were informed that they could eat outside of these times if necessary (e.g., due to uncomfortable hunger or other constraints) and were asked to record any such occasions. As in the Nottingham protocol, Irregularity was manipulated with the number and timing of meals scheduled each day. To enhance the relevance of the protocol to FI, the meal schedule in the Irregular condition was chosen to mimic the statistical features of meal timing observed in individuals experiencing FI based on analyses of 24-hour dietary recalls (Nettle & Bateson, 2019; Shinwell et al., 2021). Irregularity was quantified with three variables: mean variance in the time intervals between meals within each day, variance in the time of the first meal each day and variance in the number of meals each day. The design of the Regular and Irregular eating schedules is described in detail in the Supplementary Methods. Summary statistics for the Regular and Irregular schedules are provided in Table 1. Note. SD = standard deviation. These statistics were calculated for the specific version of the irregular schedule used in the current pilot study detailed in the Supplementary Methods.

Participants were either informed or uncertain about the upcoming schedule of daily meals over the 2-week intervention period. In the Informed condition, they were provided with the full schedule of mealtimes each day at the start of the 2-week intervention as well as being reminded of each meal via a push notification to their smartphone at the start of each 30-minute window when they were scheduled to eat. In the Uncertain condition, participants were only informed of when they were scheduled to eat via push notifications sent to their phone at the start of each eating window. All participants received the notifications, thus the only difference between the Informed and Uncertain groups was the provision of advance information about the eating schedule in the Informed group provided at the beginning of each 2-week intervention period.

In both conditions, the start notifications contained the following text, 'You are now in one of your designated eating periods. Consume any food or drinks you wish to in the next 30 minutes (note: water can be consumed at any time and does not have to be restricted to this period). Please click "OK" below to indicate that you have received this notification'. At the end of each scheduled eating window, participants were asked to confirm (via another push notification) whether they had eaten during the preceding 30 mins. The end notifications contained the following text, 'You have just had one of your designated eating periods. Please select an option below to let us know if you had something to eat or drink (note: do not count water, which can be consumed at any time): I had something to eat/drink; I chose not to eat/drink; I was unable to eat/drink; I forgot to eat/drink'. Push notifications and associated data collection were implemented using the Ethica Data mobile app for ecological momentary assessment (EMA; now Avicenna; https://avicennaresearch.com/). There was no monitoring or feedback given on the use of the app during the interventions and there was no performance-linked incentive for engagement or compliance with the app.

During eating windows, total energy intake, meal size and diet quality were not controlled or specified (as in Farshchi et al., 2004 Farshchi et al., , 2005) ) and were measured as additional outcome variables. The only exception to this was that a standardised evening meal (a macaroni cheese ready meal and chocolate biscuits comprising: 45% energy from carbohydrate, 38% protein, 15% fat and 2% fibre; 3275 kJ) was provided for the evening meal prior to each lab visit.

2.6.

Procedure Potential participants were sent an electronic copy of the participant information sheet via email and invited to attend an in-person screening visit to assess eligibility to take part. During the screening visit they were given a physical copy of the participant information sheet, had the opportunity to discuss the study and ask questions, and completed the screening questionnaire. They were weighed and their height was measured.

Eligible participants completed the consent form and then installed the EMA app on their smartphone and used it for a one-day familiarisation period before the first lab visit.

On the evening before each lab visit, participants consumed the standardised evening meal (provided at the previous visit, or at screening for visit 1) at ~18:00 and then fasted overnight, consuming only water on the morning of the visit. They were also asked to avoid alcohol and intensive exercise for 24 h beforehand.

All four lab visits followed the same protocol (Figure 1B). On arrival, participants were reminded of the timeline for the visit, asked standard compliance questions and weighed. Visits were kept quiet and controlled: access to phones was restricted and work was not permitted, and between measurements participants remained on the bed and could read nonstimulating material provided. A fingertip blood sample and a battery of computerised cognitive tests were also collected (Figure 1B); these data are not reported here.

At the end of visits 1 and 3, participants were given the instruction booklet for the forthcoming intervention (including their Intake24 log-in details) and an ActiGraph wrist monitor (data not reported owing to equipment failure), and the EMA app was set up with the forthcoming schedule. At the end of visits 2 and 4, the ActiGraph was returned and participants completed the post-intervention questionnaire. At visit 4, participants additionally completed a post-trial questionnaire, were debriefed and received their gift voucher.

2.7.

Measured variables

The questionnaires, data, codebook and R script are available on the Open Science Framework project associated with this study: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/AKWGP. Details of questionnaire scoring and subscale construction are provided in the accompanying codebook.

Measures used to evaluate the protocol (Part A) were collected during and immediately after each intervention: momentary assessment of engagement and compliance, 24-hour dietary recalls to verify that the irregularity manipulation altered the pattern of eating, and the post-intervention and post-trial questionnaires on participants' experience of the schedules, including worry about meal timing as a check on the uncertainty manipulation. Outcome measures (Part B) were collected at the lab visits, with the exception of habitual energy and macronutrient intake, which were extracted from the dietary recalls.

2.7.1 Momentary assessment of schedule compliance

During the two-week interventions participants received a push notification at the start and end of each 30-minute scheduled eating window (see section 2.5) that requested a response. Two measures of engagement with the protocol were calculated from the EMA response data: the percentage of start notifications that participants acknowledged receiving and the percentage of end notifications that participants responded to in any way. The percentage of end notifications responded to in which participants confirmed that they had eaten something during the window was calculated as a measure of self-reported momentary compliance with the eating schedules. The percentages of end notifications responded to in which participants reported that they had chosen not to eat, were unable to eat or forgot to eat were calculated to understand reasons for lack of compliance. Overall engagement/compliance percentages were pooled across all notifications. Condition-level values (Table S2) are means across participants of each participant's mean daily percentage. 2.7.2 Habitual food intake On the final three days of each intervention period 24-hour dietary recalls were collected with the Intake24 online tool (Bradley et al., 2016). Recalls were requested by push notification. Data entered more than one day after the intervention had ended were excluded.

For any reported foods that were missing from the Intake24 database, we selected the closest match manually. Since ad libitum water intake was permitted during the intervention, Intake24 entries classified as water (tap or bottled) were excluded prior to analysis. Entries classified as dietary supplements (vitamins and minerals) were also excluded.

To measure compliance with the schedules, the same summary statistics used to generate and describe the schedules (see Table 1) were calculated for each participant in each condition from their Intake24 data. Total energy intake (kJ) and intake of carbohydrate (g), protein (g), fat (g) and fibre (g) were additionally extracted for each participant in each condition.

2.7.3 Post-intervention questionnaire

At the lab visit following each 2-week intervention participants completed an 8-item questionnaire designed to probe their subjective experiences: (Q1) the effort following the schedule, (Q2) their adherence to the schedule, (Q3) the likely acceptability of sustaining the schedule for 4 weeks, (Q4) the likely acceptability of maintaining it for 8 weeks, (Q5) the impact the schedule had on the amount of food eaten, (Q6) the impact on the balance of the diet, (Q7) the frequency of uncomfortable hunger and (Q8) the degree of worry about meal timing. Each question was analysed separately. 2.7.4 Post-trial acceptability questionnaire At the end of the final lab visit participants rated their experience of the study procedures as a whole on six 5-point items, including how much they liked the lab visits, the effort required to report their diet via Intake24 and to engage with Ethica, and how helpful Ethica and the study instruction booklet were for keeping track of study requirements (Table S10). Each item was summarised descriptively. 2.7.5 Indirect calorimetry At each lab visit, expired gases were sampled and analysed using the GEM metabolic analyser (GEMNutrition, UK). Expired gases were collected once in the fasted state (assigned to t = 0 for analysis) and then every 30 min from t = 30 to 180 min after a standardised breakfast (Figure 1B). The breakfast comprised 50 g porridge oats cooked in 260 g whole milk, served with 40 g Greek-style natural yoghurt and 15 g honey (53% energy from carbohydrate, 14% protein, 33% fat; 1887 kJ). During each 15-min collection, participants lay relaxed but awake in a supine position under a metabolic hood; the first 5 min were discarded and analyses used the final 10 min. Mean values were calculated for: energy expenditure (represented as kJ/min and kJ/day), VO2, VCO2, respiratory exchange ratio (RER, computed as VCO2/ VO2), oxidation rates fat and carbohydrate (calculated using the Frayn equation (1983) assuming negligible protein oxidation), and DIT (calculated as the net incremental area under the postprandial EE curve above the fasted (t = 0) resting EE value (net iAUC), computed by the trapezoidal rule across the 0-180 min window).

One-minute mean data were excluded if they were deemed non-physiological: negative values for carbohydrate or fat oxidation rates and RER values outside the range 0.7-1.2. For analysis we separated the fasted values of RER, fat oxidation and CHO oxidation measured at t = 0 min from the postprandial values measured at 30-180 min. Thus, with REE and DIT, the indirect calorimetry yielded 8 outcome variables in total, 4 measured in the fasted state and 4 postprandially. DIT was the sole preregistered metabolic outcome.

2.7.6 Mood and motivation questionnaires

At each lab visit symptoms of generalised anxiety measured with GAD-7 (Spitzer et al., 2006) and depression measured with PHQ-9 (Kroenke et al., 2001) were preregistered outcomes and refer to the two-week period corresponding exactly to each intervention. For GAD-7 and PHQ-9, both the follow-up score and the baseline covariate were square-root transformed. The Profile of Mood States (POMS; McNair et al., 1992) and the Bond-Lader visual analogue scales (Bond & Lader, 1974) were additional, exploratory mood measures. POMS asks how the participant has felt over 'the past week including today' and yields a Total Mood Disturbance score (TMD), where lower scores indicate more stable mood profiles. The Bond-Lader scales yield three scores for instantaneous subjective feelings: alertness, calmness, and contentedness, where lower scores indicate greater alertness, calmness and contentedness. Alertness and calmness primarily index the arousal dimension of affective state, whereas contentedness indexes its valence and is therefore the dimension most directly comparable to GAD-7 and PHQ-9. The four instruments are therefore overlapping, but not identical, indices of affective state. To aid interpretation of the calmness results, we also fitted the calmness model separately to its two constituent items (Calm-Excited and Tense-Relaxed). Self-reported motivation to move and rest were measured using the CRAVE scale (Stults-Kolehmainen et al., 2021). 2.7.7 Anthropometry At screening and each lab visit body weight (kg) was measured with shoes and outer layers of clothing removed, and after being encouraged to void. On visit 1 participants were asked to wear the same clothes to each visit. Height (m) was measured at screening and checked at the first lab visit. BMI was computed as kg•m -2 . 2.7.8 Appetite scores At each lab visit self-reported appetite was measured using four 100-mm visual analogue scales (VAS): How hungry are you? How full are you? How strong is your desire to eat? How much do you think you could eat right now? (Flint et al., 2000). Scales were completed at seven time points at each visit: once in the fasted state (t = 0) and then every 30 min after the standardised breakfast (t = 30-180 min; Figure 1B). The four VAS item scores were strongly correlated within participants (Bakdash & Marusich, 2017), so the mean of the four scores at each time point was computed as a single composite appetite score, with the fullness score reversed (Dakin et al., 2026; Holliday & Blannin, 2017). For analysis, we separated the fasted VAS score (t = 0) from the six postprandial scores. 2.7.9 Ad libitum intake At each lab visit food intake was measured objectively at t = 240 min (Figure 1B). Participants were provided with a homogeneous pasta-based, nutrient-balanced ad libitum test meal (50% energy from carbohydrate, 35% fat, 15% protein; energy density 7.49 kJ•g -1 ) (Deighton et al., 2016). Participants were instructed to eat until "satisfyingly full". To avoid an empty bowl providing a cue for the cessation of eating prior to satiation (Wansink, 2004), individual portion-sized bowls were replaced with a fresh bowl before being emptied (Deighton et al., 2016). Food was consumed in isolation, free from distraction or food-related cues, and with no time limit. Total intake was measured in grams, from which energy intake was calculated.

2.8.

Data analysis

Part A outcomes were evaluated descriptively against the feasibility criteria specified in the preregistration, namely drop-out of ≤ 20% after the first lab visit and engagement with ≥ 80% of momentary-assessment notifications, and with the LMMs described below to test whether engagement, compliance and the realised pattern of meals differed between conditions as intended.

Data were analysed in R (version 4.5.2). Unless otherwise specified, outcome variables were analysed with linear mixed-effects models (LMM) fitted by restricted maximum likelihood with the R package lme4 (Bates et al., 2015). Models included fixed effects of uncertainty (Informed vs. Uncertain), manipulated between participants, and irregularity (Regular vs. Irregular), manipulated within participants, and the uncertainty × irregularity interaction. For variables measured at both baseline and follow-up, the follow-up measurement (i.e., from visits 2 and 4) was used as the outcome variable and the mean-centred value measured at baseline (visits 1 and 3), was included as a continuous covariate. For postprandial measurements (30-180 min), the baseline covariate was the mean of the postprandial values at the corresponding baseline visit; fasted values were adjusted for the fasted baseline value. To control for non-independence due to the repeated-measures structure of the data, all models included a random intercept for participant. Where a variable was measured multiple times within a visit (substrate oxidation measures and appetite VAS scores), an additional random intercept was included for visit.

Fixed effects were evaluated using Type III F-tests, computed with the R package afex (Singmann et al., 2012). Sum-to-zero contrasts were applied to the categorical predictors so that tests of the main effects estimate average effects across the levels of the other factor. In a departure from the preregistration, denominator degrees of freedom were approximated using the Kenward-Roger method that yields marginally more conservative tests in small samples (Kenward & Roger, 1997). Fixed effect estimates were considered statistically significant at p < .050. We report full model output for all dependent variables in supplementary tables and, in the main text, describe in detail only those effects that were statistically significant or marginal (p < .100), indicating in each case whether the analysis was preregistered or exploratory.

To complement conventional null hypothesis significance testing, and to distinguish genuine equivalence from an inconclusive result due to limited statistical power, we conducted preregistered equivalence testing following the two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure (Lakens et al., 2018). A region of practical equivalence (ROPE) was defined as ± 0.1 SD, corresponding to a negligible effect size. The equivalence p-value is the TOST pvalue, i.e. the larger of the two one-sided p-values. A result is equivalent if the 90% CI lies within the ROPE, a meaningful difference if it lies wholly outside, otherwise undecided. 2.8.1 Missing values Of the 336 EE measurements (12 participants × 4 visits × 7 timepoints), 19 (5.7%) were missing. One participant lost an entire follow-up visit (all seven EE measurements) to an equipment failure. Since this loss was completely at random, the visit was excluded; the LMMs described above used all of that participant's remaining visits. The other 12 missing values (3.6%) were sporadic measurements within otherwise-complete curves, but included four missing t = 0 values, precluding simple interpolation. These sporadic missing values were handled by multiple imputation using the mice package. Imputation was carried out at the level of the individual measurements using multivariate imputation by chained equations with predictive mean matching. Each visit's seven timepoints were arranged as columns (one row per visit), and each missing value was imputed from the other six timepoints of the same curve together with uncertainty, irregularity, intervention period, visit type (baseline or follow-up), and body weight at the visit and at screening; participant ID was not used as a predictor. Fifty imputed datasets were generated. Resting EE and the net iAUC were then computed within each imputed dataset, and all subsequent models were fitted separately to each before pooling.

The resulting estimates were combined using Rubin's rules (using the package mitml). Fixed effects were evaluated as Type III F-tests (as described above). Under multiple imputation, each effect was tested by comparing the full model with the model omitting that single term, combining these comparisons across the imputed datasets with the D1 multivariate Wald statistic, the multiple-imputation analogue of the Type III F-test. Because the fraction of missing information was very low, the default large-sample pooled degrees of freedom were implausibly large for a study of this size. The small-sample adjustment of Reiter (2007) was therefore applied, using complete-data denominator degrees of freedom taken from the corresponding Kenward-Roger model fitted to a completed dataset. For presentation, estimated marginal means and their 95% confidence intervals were computed for each condition within every imputed dataset and pooled across imputations by the same rules. The preregistered equivalence tests for the DIT models were likewise applied to the pooled parameter estimates: the 90% confidence intervals used in the two one-sided tests were constructed from the Rubin-pooled estimates and standard errors on the same Barnard-Rubin (Kenward-Roger) degrees of freedom, with the region of practical equivalence set to ±0.1 SD of the outcome.

3. Results

>Results

3.1.

Part A: Feasibility, acceptability and fidelity of the protocol 3.1.1 Participants, recruitment and retention Participant flow through the experiment is summarised in Figure 2. Twenty-five women expressed interest and were assessed for eligibility, of whom 11 were excluded. Eight did not meet the inclusion criteria (four had a BMI outside the healthy range, two had an existing medical condition, one had a GAD-7 score ≥ 10, and one had a USDA food-security score ≥ 2) and three declined to participate. Eligible participants were sequentially allocated to the four groups in the prespecified random sequence. There were two withdrawals after the first lab visit (one Informed and one Uncertain); these were replaced with two new participants who completed the entire protocol. Thus, the drop-out rate following the first lab visit was 14.3%, within the preregistered feasibility criterion of ≤ 20%. Twelve participants completed the entire protocol and were included in the analyses.

At screening, the 12 included participants were 27.4 ± 6.8 (mean ± SD) years of age, had a BMI of 21.61 ± 2.79 kg•m -2 , a PHQ-9 score of 3.00 ± 1.21 and a GAD-7 score of 3.25 ± 1.86 (Table S1).

Descriptive statistics for all outcome variables are reported as mean (SD) for each of the four design cells (Informed-Regular, Informed-Irregular, Uncertain-Regular, Uncertain-Irregular). Variables measured either during the intervention periods (EMA and Intake24), or only after the intervention ended (post-intervention questionnaire responses), are reported as a single mean for each cell (Table S2), whereas variables measured at both baseline and follow-up (indirect calorimetry, mood, motivation, body weight, and appetite variables) are reported as means for each time point (Tables S3-S5). Where the baseline measurement was included as a covariate in analyses, it predicted the follow-up value for most outcomes, indicating consistency of measurements within participants; these effects are reported in the tables and not described further.

3.1.2 Engagement and compliance: momentary assessment (preregistered)

Overall engagement with the push notifications delivered at the start and end of eating windows was 80.2% and 80.9% respectively, meeting the preregistered threshold for good engagement (≥ 80%). If a participant responded to an end notification, overall self-reported momentary compliance with the eating schedules was 78.4%. Reasons selected for lack of compliance were: chose not to eat 14.6%, unable to eat 6.2% and forgot to eat 0.8%.

Preregistered LMMs were fitted to evaluate the effects of uncertainty and irregularity on engagement and compliance with day of intervention as a covariate to test for changes over time (Table S6). For the percentage of start notifications responded to, there were no significant effects of uncertainty or irregularity, either as main effects or in interaction, but there was a significant effect of day, whereby engagement declined by an estimated 0.9% per day over each two-week intervention period (F(1, 321) = 14.15, p < .001). The results were similar for the percentage of responses to end notifications (b = -0.8%, F(1, 321) = 10.53, p = .001). For self-reported percentage compliance with the eating schedules, there were no significant effects of uncertainty or irregularity, either as main effects or in interaction, and no significant effect of day (all p > .110).

3.1.3 Fidelity of the irregularity manipulation: 24-hour dietary recalls (exploratory)

Descriptive statistics for the observed meal patterns and those expected given the schedule on days 11-13 are shown in Table 2. Although the observed differences between the Regular and Irregular condition are smaller than scheduled, they differ in the expected direction, with the observed pattern of meals being more variable in the Irregular condition, as intended. Figure 3A shows the distribution of meals reported across the day in the Regular and Irregular conditions. Clear peaks are evident in the Regular condition at the five scheduled mealtimes, with 75.0% of meals occurring at the scheduled times. In contrast, in the Irregular condition, meals were more evenly distributed across the day, with only 14.9% occurring at the times scheduled in the Regular condition (for comparison, these numbers should be 100.0% and 11.1% respectively for days 11-13 if participants adhered perfectly to the specified eating schedules on those days). Note. Observed behaviour was extracted from Intake24 recalls requested for days 11-13 of each intervention period, but some of the recalls likely correspond to day 14. Meals reported at the same time (one incidence) were treated as separate meals with an inter-meal interval of 0 min. The cleaned dataset comprised 55 of the 72 24-hour recalls requested, yielding details on a total of 233 meals; n indicates the number of participants contributing data in each condition. One participant in the Informed condition is entirely excluded due to data being submitted too late and another participant had no data for the Regular condition. Statistics shown are mean (SD) for participants. The scheduled behaviour columns show the expected statistics if participants followed the reporting instructions and meal schedules for days 11-13 perfectly.

LMMs were fitted to examine whether the irregularity manipulation caused the intended effects on meal patterns (Table S7). Supporting the difference in Figure 3A, the percentage of meals reported consumed at any of the five times scheduled in the Regular condition was significantly higher during the Regular condition compared to the Irregular condition (F(1,45.80) = 94.63, p < .001; Figure 3B). As intended, there was no difference in the mean number of meals consumed each day between the Regular and Irregular conditions (F(1,43.88) = 0.06, p = .803; Figure 3C). The mean within-day standard deviation in the time gap between meals was significantly higher in the Irregular condition compared to the Regular condition (F(1,41.95) = 7.95, p = .007; Figure 3D). The between-day standard deviation in the time of the first meal of the day was also significantly higher in the Irregular condition (F(1,9.42) = 6.40, p = .031; Figure 3E). Finally, while the between-day standard deviation in the number of meals reported per day was higher in the Irregular condition, this difference was not significant in the subset of days for which 24-hour recalls were recorded (F(1,9.32) = 1.05, p = .332; Figure 3F). Analysis of overall total daily energy intake and macronutrient intake from the 24-hour recalls revealed that participants reported consuming 6886 ± 1286 kJ per day. Reported macronutrient intake per day was: 72.30 ± 32.64 g protein, 193.74 ± 25.75 g carbohydrate, 66.62 ± 19.59 g fat and 17.79 ± 6.86 g fibre (mean ± SD). These values were close to National Diet and Nutrition Survey (NDNS) reference values for adult women in the UK obtained using similar self-report methodology (Public Health England et al., 2020; data from 2016/17-2018/19 for women aged 19-64 years)(Table S8).

3.1.4 Acceptability and fidelity of the uncertainty manipulation: post-intervention questionnaire (exploratory)

Median responses indicated the participants found following the prescribed meal schedule some effort (Q1: median = 3), but they reported following it almost always (75-99%; Q2: median = 4). They agreed that they could have followed the schedule for four weeks (Q3: median = 4). However, they neither agreed nor disagreed whether they could have followed it for eight weeks (Q4: median = 3). They reported eating the same amount as usual (Q5: median = 3), with no change to the balance of their diet (Q6: median = 3). They reported feeling uncomfortably hungry on only 1-3 days (Q7: median = 2) and they were not at all worried about when they would next eat (Q8: median = 1).

LMMs were fitted to test the effects of uncertainty and irregularity on the responses to each of the eight questions (Table S9). Participants' responses were significantly affected by uncertainty and irregularity for two questions only. For the effort required to follow the recommended meal timing (Q1), there was a significant interaction between uncertainty × irregularity with effort rated as higher in the Uncertain-Irregular condition compared to the other three conditions (F(1,7.10) = 7.98, p = .025; Figure 4A). For worry about meal timing (Q8), there were significant main effects of uncertainty and irregularity, with worry rated as higher in the Uncertain and Irregular conditions (F(1,7.93) = 14.18, p = .006; F(1,7.93) = 9.93, p = .014 respectively; Figure 4B). The effect of uncertainty on worry indicates that the withholding of advance information about the schedule was registered by participants.

3.1.5 Acceptability of the study procedures: post-trial questionnaire (exploratory)

Nine of the 12 participants completed the post-trial acceptability questionnaire; the other three were not given it due to experimenter error. Responses were generally favourable (Table S10). Seven of nine participants liked or strongly liked the testing visits, and none disliked them. Most reported little or no effort in engaging with Ethica (six of nine), and most agreed that Ethica (seven of nine) and the instruction booklet (eight of nine) helped them keep track of study requirements. Dietary reporting via Intake24 was the most effortful component (median rating 3, 'some effort'), with four of nine participants reporting little or no effort.

The Part A outcomes are summarised in Table 3 against the preregistered feasibility criteria and the intended effects of the two manipulations.
