3.2.

Part B: Effects of the intervention on outcome variables The preregistered tests of the effects of the manipulations on DIT, GAD-7 and PHQ-9 are summarised in Table 4; all other analyses of outcomes were exploratory.

3.2.1 Indirect calorimetry

Energy expenditure (DIT preregistered, REE exploratory) Across all conditions, energy expenditure (EE) rose and then declined over the three-hour postprandial period, confirming a clear thermic response to the meal (LMM of follow-up EE with time point (0-180 min) as a seven-level factor and random intercepts for participant and visit: effect of time point, F(6, 129.57) = 18.59, p < .001; Figure 5A).

An LMM was fitted to explore the effects of uncertainty and irregularity on resting energy expenditure (REE, the fasted value at t = 0 min) at follow-up, controlling for REE at baseline. REE was not significantly affected by uncertainty or irregularity, either as main effects or in interaction (Table S11). DIT was the primary preregistered outcome variable. We predicted lower DIT following irregular meals and an interaction, with DIT lowest when meals were both uncertain and irregular (the amplification hypothesis). An LMM controlling for the participant's baseline DIT showed that neither prediction was supported (Table 4; Table S11). The uncertainty × irregularity interaction was marginal (F(1, 8.08) = 4.20, p = .074), but its form was different from the prediction: rather than being lowest when meals were both Uncertain and Irregular, DIT was highest in the Informed-Regular condition and lower in the other three (Figure 5B; Table S3). There was also no main effect of irregularity in the preregistered replication model with irregularity as the sole independent variable (Table 4; Table S11). Preregistered equivalence tests on these effects were all undecided (Table 4). [-0.26, 0.09] Undecided Note. F-tests are Type III tests with Kenward-Roger denominator degrees of freedom; for diet-induced thermogenesis they are pooled across 50 multiply imputed datasets (D1 statistic with small-sample adjusted degrees of freedom). Coefficients (b) use sum-to-zero ±1 coding with Irregular = +1 and Uncertain = +1, so a positive b means higher values in the Irregular/Uncertain condition. A 90% confidence interval (CI) is used in the two one-sided equivalence tests; ROPE = region of practical equivalence (±0.1 SD of the outcome). Decision = outcome of the equivalence test; Undecided = the 90% CI overlaps the ROPE boundary. Baseline covariates are reported in Tables S11 and S15.

Substrate oxidation (exploratory) Postprandial respiratory exchange ratio (RER), fat oxidation and carbohydrate oxidation all changed significantly over time (RER: F(5, 89.22) = 4.03, p = .002; fat oxidation: F(5, 89.35) = 3.84, p = .003; CHO oxidation: F(5, 89.21) = 5.34, p < .001), confirming the expected metabolic response to the meal. There were no significant main effects of uncertainty or irregularity (all p > .340). The irregularity × uncertainty × time interaction was significant for RER (F(5, 89.20) = 2.60, p = .030), fat oxidation (F(5, 89.31) = 2.77, p = .022) and carbohydrate oxidation (F(5, 89.20) = 2.33, p = .049), indicating that the influence of irregularity on the postprandial trajectory depended on the uncertainty condition. No manipulation effects were significant in the fasted state (all p > .120; Tables S12-S14).

3.2.2 Mood and motivation questionnaires

For each of the six mood variables, an LMM was fitted to explore the effects of uncertainty and irregularity on mood at follow-up, controlling for the participant's measurement at baseline (Figure 6; Table 4; Table S15). Anxiety and depression symptoms (GAD-7 and PHQ-9; preregistered) We preregistered a main effect of uncertainty, with more self-reported symptoms of anxiety (GAD-7) and depression (PHQ-9) when food intake was uncertain, and an interaction, with the highest anxiety and depression scores when food intake was both irregular and uncertain. Descriptively, for both GAD-7 and PHQ-9, the scores at follow-up indicated the most negative affective states following the Uncertain-Irregular intervention and the most positive states following the Informed-Regular intervention, with the greatest improvement from baseline in the Informed-Regular condition and little or no change in the other three (Table S5). However, when controlling for baseline scores there was no significant effect of uncertainty or irregularity on either GAD-7 or PHQ-9, either as main effects or in interaction (all p > .050; Table 4; Table S15). Preregistered equivalence tests on these effects were all undecided (Table 4). Profile of Mood States (exploratory) For total mood disturbance, there was no significant effect of uncertainty or irregularity, either as main effects or in interaction (all p > .050; Table S15). Bond-Lader affective state (exploratory) For alertness, neither manipulation nor their interaction had a significant effect (Table S15). For calmness, there was a significant main effect of uncertainty (F(1, 9.76) = 8.83, p = .014), with lower calmness scores, indicating greater calmness, in the Uncertain condition; the uncertainty × irregularity interaction was marginal (F(1, 9.85) = 3.35, p = .098). In models fitted to the two calmness items separately, the effect of uncertainty was significant for Calm-Excited (F(1, 9.13) = 7.82, p = .021) and marginal for Tense-Relaxed (F(1, 9.70) = 4.70, p = .056). For contentedness (the valence dimension) there were significant effects of irregularity (F(1, 9.67) = 6.55, p = .029) and of the uncertainty × irregularity interaction (F(1, 11.35) = 5.77, p = .034). Contentedness improved most (i.e., scores were lowest) following the Informed-Regular intervention, whereas the other three conditions showed little improvement or a decline; the interaction reflected that the advantage of Regular over Irregular meals was present in the Informed condition but absent in the Uncertain condition (Table S15; Table S5). Motivation to rest and move (CRAVE) (exploratory) Neither the rest nor the move score was significantly affected by uncertainty or irregularity, either as main effects or in interaction (all p > .433; Table S16).

3.2.3 Appetite VAS scores (exploratory)

Fasted appetite was high (estimated marginal means 65-76 mm on the 100-mm scale), but there were no significant effects of uncertainty or irregularity on fasted appetite at follow-up, either as main effects or in interaction, controlling for fasted appetite at baseline (Table S17).

An LMM was fitted to explore the effect of uncertainty, irregularity and time point (30-180 mins post breakfast) on postprandial appetite, adjusting for the baseline-visit postprandial mean (Table S18; Figure 7). Appetite rose steadily across the postprandial period (F(5, 100) = 33.35, p < .001), increasing from roughly 15-30 mm at 30 min to 44-54 mm at 180 min. Neither uncertainty nor irregularity had a main effect on postprandial appetite, and none of the condition × time interactions were significant, indicating that the shape of appetite recovery did not differ between conditions. The uncertainty × irregularity interaction was marginal (F(1, 10.16) = 3.54, p = .089): regular meal timing was associated with lower postprandial appetite when participants were informed of the schedule but not when timing was uncertain.

3.2.4 Habitual energy and macronutrient intake (exploratory)

An LMM was fitted to explore the effects of uncertainty and irregularity on total daily energy intake, controlling for participant height and weight at screening. The main effects of uncertainty and irregularity were not significant, but there was a significant interaction (F(1,44.13) = 9.80, p = .003) whereby the Irregular condition increased energy intake relative to the Regular condition in the Uncertain group, but decreased it in the Informed group (Table S19; Figure 8A). LMMs were also fitted to explore the effects of uncertainty and irregularity on intake of each of the four macronutrients, controlling for total daily energy intake. As expected, there was a significant association between total energy intake and intake of each macronutrient, but there were no significant effects of uncertainty or irregularity on intake of any macronutrient (all p > .070; Table S19).

3.2.5 Ad libitum intake of standardised meal (exploratory)

An LMM was fitted to explore the effect of uncertainty and irregularity on ad libitum intake of the standardised lunch controlling for ad libitum intake at the baseline visit. There was no main effect of uncertainty, but a significant main effect of irregularity (F(1, 9.10) = 10.90, p = .009) and a significant uncertainty × irregularity interaction (F(1, 9.49) = 8.43, p = .017). Participants consumed more following the Irregular intervention in the Informed condition (F(1, 4.58) = 17.62, p = .010), but there was no effect of irregularity in the Uncertain condition (F(1, 4.03) = 0.56, p = .496; Table S20; Figure 8B).

3.2.6 Body weight (exploratory)

Body weight was not significantly affected by uncertainty or irregularity, either as main effects or in interaction (all p > .450; Table S21).

3.2.7 Condition structure across all outcomes (exploratory)

With only 12 participants, the formal test of the uncertainty × irregularity interaction had little power to distinguish between the different ways in which the two manipulations might combine. We therefore asked, for each outcome, which of four simple patterns best described the means of the four conditions (Figure 9). In the No effect pattern, all four conditions have the same mean. In the Threshold pattern, the Informed-Regular condition differs from the other three, which do not differ from one another; that is, either irregularity or uncertainty alone is enough to produce the full effect. In the Additive pattern, irregularity and uncertainty each have their own effect, and the two effects sum when both are present. In the Amplification pattern (our preregistered hypothesis), the two factors interact, so that all four conditions can differ. These patterns range from the simplest to the most complex, requiring 0, 1, 2 and 3 additional parameters respectively. We fitted each pattern as a model and compared the models using AICc, which rewards a model for fitting the data well but penalises it for complexity, so a more complex pattern is preferred only if it describes the data substantially better than a simpler one. Each outcome was classified according to its best-supported model if that model was better than the next-best by at least 2 AICc, and as Undecided otherwise.

All four models included the outcome's covariates and were fitted by maximum likelihood; the two energy-expenditure outcomes were fitted within each of the 50 imputed datasets and their AICc values averaged. Postprandial outcomes were summarised as the mean of the 30-180 min values at each visit, with the corresponding baseline-visit mean as the covariate, and dietary-intake outcomes as participant × condition means, with energy intake adjusted for height and body weight at screening and macronutrient intakes adjusted for energy intake. Across all 29 outcomes the Amplification model was never the best-supported, so the pattern required by our preregistered hypothesis, and indeed any pattern in which all four conditions differ, was not supported for any outcome (Table 5). Three outcomes were classified as Threshold: habitual energy intake, ad libitum test-meal intake, and Bond-Lader contentedness, for which the Threshold model out-fitted the No effect model by 4.17, 4.97 and 5.76 AICc respectively. For 15 outcomes the No effect model was clearly best (by at least 2 AICc), and the remaining 11 were Undecided, with the leading model (No effect, Threshold or, for one outcome, Additive) within 2 AICc of the next-best.

The 15 no-effect outcomes spanned every domain: resting energy expenditure, all three fasted substrate-oxidation measures and postprandial carbohydrate oxidation, all four macronutrients, GAD-7 and alertness, the two CRAVE motivational scales, and two of the four questionnaire items. Among the 11 undecided outcomes, the No effect model led narrowly for six (body weight, calmness, postprandial appetite, postprandial RER and fat oxidation, and hunger), the Threshold model led for four (DIT, PHQ-9, POMS total mood disturbance and fasted appetite), and the Additive model narrowly led for worry about meal timing.

Since the Threshold model led for two of the three preregistered outcomes (DIT and PHQ-9), we also tested the contrast between the Informed-Regular condition and the other three conditions jointly across all three preregistered outcomes (DIT, GAD-7 and PHQ-9) in an exploratory pooled analysis. Each outcome's follow-up score was adjusted for its baseline covariate and z-scored, with GAD-7 and PHQ-9 scores sign-reversed so that higher values on the combined scale indicated higher DIT and lower symptom scores. The three outcomes were then modelled together, with fixed effects of outcome and the contrast and a random intercept for participant. Across the three outcomes, the Informed-Regular condition differed significantly from the other three conditions in the direction of higher DIT and lower anxiety and depression scores (F(1, 62.90) = 6.92, p = .011), and there was no evidence that this difference varied between outcomes (outcome × contrast: F(2, 52.19) = 0.46, p = .632; Table S22).

Individually, the same contrast was marginal for DIT and PHQ-9 and not significant for GAD-7 (Table S23). For substrate oxidation, the group × time interaction was significant for fat and carbohydrate oxidation and marginal for RER (RER: F(5, 99.13) = 2.03, p = .080; fat oxidation: F(5, 99.18) = 2.38, p = .044; carbohydrate oxidation: F(5, 99.13) = 2.32, p = .049; Figure 10; Tables S12-S14): relative to Informed-Regular, the other three conditions showed a lower thermic response to the meal (B) and maintained higher RER (C), lower fat (D) and higher carbohydrate oxidation (E) as the meal was processed. AICc from the best-fitting model for that outcome; the best model is shown as 0.00 in bold, and the gap to the next-best model is the smallest non-zero value in the row. Classification is the bestsupported model when it leads the next-best model by at least 2 AICc, and Undecided otherwise (so where the Threshold model leads the No effect model only narrowly, e.g. DIT, PHQ-9, the classification is Undecided, not Threshold). A classification of No effect denotes that no condition structure was detected, not proof that no effect exists. AICc for the two energy-expenditure outcomes is averaged across the 50 multiply imputed datasets. Models were fitted by maximum likelihood.

4. Discussion

We developed an experimental protocol that manipulates two features of the eating patterns associated with food insecurity (FI), namely the irregularity and the uncertainty of meals, and piloted it in 12 free-living, healthy, adult women. Part A of the study achieved its objectives: the protocol proved feasible and acceptable, the irregularity manipulation produced the intended changes in the pattern of eating, and participants registered the uncertainty manipulation. To our knowledge, this is the first protocol to manipulate uncertainty about the timing of meals in humans independently of their irregularity. In Part B, none of our preregistered predictions was supported. Two weeks of irregular meals did not reduce dietinduced thermogenesis (DIT), uncertainty did not amplify any effect of irregularity on DIT, and uncertainty did not increase self-reported symptoms of anxiety or depression. However, the preregistered equivalence tests were undecided in every case, so these null results reflect the limited power of a pilot rather than evidence that the effects are absent. Exploratory analyses pointed to a different pattern from the one we predicted: where the manipulation had any detectable effect, the Informed-Regular condition tended to differ from the three conditions involving irregularity, uncertainty or both, which resembled one another. The same contrast was supported when the three preregistered outcomes were analysed together: none showed a significant difference between the Informed-Regular condition and the other three conditions on its own, but jointly they did, with no evidence that the difference varied between outcomes. We consider the feasibility and fidelity of the protocol (Part A) first, then the effects of the intervention on each group of outcomes (Part B), and finally the implications for a full trial.

4.1.

Part A: Feasibility, acceptability and fidelity of the protocol 4.1.1 Feasibility, acceptability and compliance The protocol met both of its preregistered feasibility criteria, for retention and for engagement (Table 3). Most exclusions reflected the stringent eligibility criteria rather than unwillingness to take part. Retention was high, placing the protocol in the highest band of our preregistered feasibility scheme (drop-out ≤ 20%).

Engagement with the app was at the threshold that we preregistered as indicating good engagement (≥ 80%), and self-reported momentary compliance with the schedules was marginally below the 80% threshold commonly recommended for EMA protocols (Jones et al., 2019). Most non-compliance reflected a decision not to eat rather than an inability to eat or forgetting. Neither engagement nor compliance differed between conditions, so differential adherence is unlikely to explain any condition effects. Engagement with the app did, however, decline steadily across each two-week intervention period; if this decline continued at the same rate, engagement would fall below 80% over longer interventions. Since the current protocol included no monitoring, feedback or performance-linked incentive for engagement (cf. Neal et al., 2025), these are obvious targets for improvement.

Momentary assessment minimises the recall biases that affect retrospective self-report and avoids the need for participants to summarise their own behaviour, but EMA data are unlikely to be missing at random (Stone & Shiffman, 2002). Participants might be less likely to respond at the end of an eating window if they had failed to eat during it, which would inflate our estimate of compliance. However, the very similar response rates to the start and end notifications argue against a strong bias of this kind, since acknowledging a start notification does not require the participant to report on her own behaviour.

The post-intervention questionnaire reinforced this picture. Participants reported following the schedule almost always, reported that following it required some effort, and agreed that they could have sustained the schedule for 4 weeks, though not necessarily for 8. However, the observed decline in app engagement over our two-week intervention suggests that maintaining sufficient compliance over four weeks may prove challenging. They did not report changing the amount or balance of food eaten, and uncomfortable hunger and worry about the timing of meals were reported infrequently. These are retrospective reports over a two-week period and so are subject to biases in encoding and recall, but their convergence with the momentary EMA data is reassuring. Taken together, the data suggest that the protocol was well tolerated, but that lengthening the intervention periods may test participants' willingness to continue. Results from an intensive longitudinal study of the effects of changes in FI status on GAD-7 and PHQ-9 scores suggest that 4 weeks is sufficient to see effects of FI on affective state (Bateson et al., 2025), meaning that longer interventions are not necessarily required.

The burden of the protocol was not, however, distributed evenly across conditions. The effort required to follow the schedule was rated highest in the Uncertain-Irregular condition and worry about when participants would next eat was increased by both irregularity and uncertainty, independently. A similar but only marginal pattern was apparent for uncomfortable hunger (Table S9). Although worry was low in absolute terms, this pattern implies that a full trial should anticipate that adherence and retention will be hardest to maintain in the Uncertain-Irregular condition.

4.1.2 Fidelity of the manipulations

The 24-hour dietary recalls confirmed that participants largely ate when instructed, with meals concentrated at the scheduled times in the Regular condition (Figure 3A). Critically, the recalls showed that the Irregular schedule altered the pattern of eating rather than the number of meals: the mean number of meals per day did not differ between conditions, whereas both the within-day variability in the intervals between meals and the between-day variability in the time of the first meal were significantly greater in the Irregular condition. Together with the high self-reported adherence, this evidence of a successful manipulation increases confidence that a full trial could deliver the intended contrast in eating patterns.

The realised irregularity was nevertheless smaller than scheduled, and the shortfall was not uniform across its components. Participants reported fewer meals per day than scheduled in both conditions, consistent with the EMA reports that non-compliance was mostly a choice not to eat. The between-day standard deviation in the number of meals was lower than scheduled and did not differ significantly between conditions. Thus, the component of irregularity that most directly replicates the Nottingham protocol, namely between-day variation in meal number, was the one least successfully delivered, whereas the components that we added to mimic the eating patterns of people living with FI were delivered as intended. One cause may have been the clustering of scheduled meals: because meals were assigned at random to half-hour windows, 13 of the 56 intervals between consecutive meals in the Irregular schedule were only 30 minutes long (Supplementary Methods Table 2), and participants who had just eaten may reasonably have merged sequential eating windows into a single meal. Consistent with this, the shortfall relative to the schedule was larger in the Irregular than in the Regular condition (Table 2), although EMA reports of choosing not to eat were not more frequent in the Irregular condition (Table S2). Our Irregular schedule also differed from the Nottingham protocol, which held the time of the first meal constant in both conditions and therefore, unlike FI, introduced no variance in the time of the first meal. Importantly, these conclusions rest on a limited sample of three days with dietary recalls at the end of each intervention.

More fundamentally, we generated the schedule to reproduce summary statistics of meal distribution common in individuals living with FI (Nettle & Bateson, 2019; Shinwell et al., 2021), but these statistics do not uniquely specify the underlying pattern. A subsequent analysis showed that people experiencing FI eat their meals at around the same times as foodsecure people but are more likely to miss or skip main meals (Bateson et al., 2026). The Nottingham protocol, which created irregularity by omitting meals from a fixed set of more regularly spaced eating times, therefore captures the structure of eating under FI better than our randomly timed schedule did in this respect.

The fidelity of the uncertainty manipulation is harder to verify, because uncertainty is a state of the person rather than a property of the pattern of meals and so cannot be extracted from dietary records. Nevertheless, worry about when participants would next eat was greater in the Uncertain than in the Informed condition, which shows that the withholding of advance information about the schedule was registered by participants as intended, even though we did not measure uncertainty about the timing of the next meal directly (see below).

In summary, Part A achieved its objectives. The protocol was feasible and acceptable, adherence did not differ between conditions, and both manipulations changed what they were designed to affect (Table 3).

4.2.

Part B: Effects of the intervention on outcomes 4.2.1 Diet-induced thermogenesis and substrate oxidation

We did not replicate the reduction in DIT following irregular meals reported in all four Nottingham studies (Alhussain et al., 2016 (Alhussain et al., , 2022;; Farshchi et al., 2004 Farshchi et al., , 2005)), and we found no support for the predicted amplification of this effect by uncertainty. The uncertainty × irregularity interaction was marginal, but its form showed a different pattern from our prediction: rather than being lowest in the Uncertain-Irregular condition, DIT was highest in the Informed-Regular condition and lower in the other three. In consequence, the effect of irregularity was in the predicted direction in the Informed condition, which most closely resembles the Nottingham protocol in that participants knew their schedules, but was largely absent in the Uncertain condition; averaging across the two diluted the main effect of irregularity contributing to the non-replication of the Nottingham protocol results.

Several differences between our protocol and the Nottingham studies might also have contributed to the failure to replicate. First, as in the two earliest Nottingham studies (Farshchi et al., 2004 (Farshchi et al., , 2005)), but unlike the two most recent (Alhussain et al., 2016 (Alhussain et al., , 2022)), food was not provided, so energy intake and diet composition were free to vary. Habitual energy intake did differ between conditions (see below), and we cannot exclude the possibility that this influenced the thermogenic response to the standardised breakfast, despite the standardised evening meal. Second, as described above, our Irregular schedule had a different temporal structure from the Nottingham schedule, and the between-day variation in the number of meals that the Nottingham protocol manipulated was attenuated in practice on the days for which we had data. Third, our schedules contained a mean of five meals per day rather than six. Finally, adding a between-participant manipulation of uncertainty halved the number of participants contributing to the within-participant comparison of Regular and Irregular meals in each uncertainty condition. Since the equivalence tests were undecided, our failure to successfully replicate the Nottingham studies should not be overinterpreted.

The exploratory substrate-oxidation data were broadly consistent with the DIT result. Irregularity altered the postprandial trajectories of respiratory exchange ratio (RER) and fat oxidation in a manner that depended on the uncertainty condition, and exploratory contrasts suggested that the Informed-Regular condition maintained lower carbohydrate and higher fat oxidation than the other three conditions as the meal was processed (Figure 10). Together with the DIT result, this pattern is directionally consistent with energy conservation and a shift in fuel partitioning towards fat storage, as predicted by the insurance hypothesis (Nettle et al., 2017) and as observed in animal models exposed to unpredictable food (Andrews et al., 2021; Bateson et al., 2021; Gil, Lund, Żylicz, Ranea-Robles, et al., 2025), but it emerged from exploratory analyses and requires confirmation.

A comparable shift in fuel use has been reported cross-sectionally in humans. In a wholeroom calorimetry study of a predominantly male inpatient sample, adults with FI had a higher 24-hour respiratory quotient than food-secure adults, reflecting higher carbohydrate and lower lipid oxidation, with no difference in 24-hour energy expenditure (Booker et al., 2022). The direction of this difference matches the postprandial pattern in our exploratory contrasts, in which the three conditions involving irregularity, uncertainty or both showed relatively higher carbohydrate and lower fat oxidation than the Informed-Regular condition. Moreover, the association with FI was clearer for 24-hour respiratory quotient, which is dominated by the fed state, than for sleeping respiratory quotient, which was associated with FI only when FI was scored as a continuous variable; this is at least compatible with our finding that the effects of the manipulation were confined to postprandial rather than fasted substrate oxidation. Booker et al. (2022) measured substrate oxidation after at least four days of a weight-maintaining diet meaning that the differences they observed cannot be attributed to current energy balance or diet composition, but because their design was cross-sectional they could reflect longer-term correlates of FI rather than an effect of FI itself. An experimental manipulation such as ours avoids this problem. The interpretation of such a shift, however, differs between theoretical frameworks. Friedman et al. (2024) regard a redirection of fuel from oxidation towards storage as a disorder of fuel partitioning that initiates obesity, with increased energy intake and reduced expenditure as compensatory consequences, and they list FI among the potential causes of obesity whose effects on fuel partitioning merit investigation. Under the insurance hypothesis, by contrast, the same shift would be an adaptive response to cues that the future food supply is unpredictable (Bateson & Pepper, 2023). One implication of the adaptive view is that the shift should be inducible in people with no pre-existing metabolic disorder simply by making their meals irregular or uncertain, which is what our protocol is designed to test. Given that our substrate-oxidation results were exploratory, we regard the convergence with Booker et al. (2022) as suggestive only, but it identifies postprandial fuel partitioning as a candidate outcome for a confirmatory trial. 4.2.2 Anxiety, depression and affective state Contrary to our preregistered predictions, uncertainty did not increase symptoms of anxiety or depression, and the equivalence tests were again undecided. The exploratory measures nevertheless showed a consistent pattern: for the three measures indexing the valence of affective state (PHQ-9, POMS total mood disturbance and Bond-Lader contentedness), the Threshold model, in which the Informed-Regular condition differs from the other three, was the best-supported, decisively so for contentedness. This coherence lends some weight to an otherwise weak set of individual results.

Two further aspects of the mood data merit comment. First, uncertainty produced a significant main effect on the calmness subscale, in the direction of greater calmness in the Uncertain condition, which is opposite to the direction expected and to the greater worry about meal timing reported by participants in this condition. Since the effect was stronger for the Calm-Excited item than for Tense-Relaxed, it may partly reflect lower activation, which would be compatible with a low-energy response to unpredictable food (Bateson et al., 2021); however, with uncertainty manipulated between participants and only six per group, it may equally reflect group differences not captured by the baseline covariate, and we do not interpret it further. Second, while uncertainty increased worry specifically about the timing of meals, there was no detectable effect on generalised anxiety measured by GAD-7. A twoweek manipulation in food-secure women who knew that it was temporary may be sufficient to generate domain-specific worry without that worry generalising.

4.2.3 Appetite and food intake

The measures of appetite and food intake did not show a consistent effect of the manipulation: retrospective self-reports showed no detectable effects, whereas the objective and momentary measures showed interactions between uncertainty and irregularity, though not always in the same direction.

In the laboratory, the measures were internally consistent within the Informed group. Following the Informed-Irregular intervention, postprandial appetite was marginally higher and ad libitum intake was significantly greater than following the Informed-Regular intervention, whereas irregularity had no detectable effect on either measure in the Uncertain group. Habitual energy intake reported in the dietary recalls also showed a significant uncertainty × irregularity interaction, but here irregularity reduced intake in the Informed group and increased it in the Uncertain group. The opposite directions of the laboratory and free-living effects in the Informed group are difficult to interpret with confidence. One speculative possibility is that reduced intake during an irregular fortnight created a modest energy deficit that was expressed as increased appetite and intake when food was freely available in the laboratory. Alternatively, the free-living result may be unreliable, because the recall data for the Informed-Regular condition came from only four participants. In addition, the scheduled number of meals per day differed between the Regular and Irregular conditions on the days covered by the recalls: it was always five in the Regular schedule but was six, nine, three and five on days 11, 12, 13 and 14 of the Irregular schedule, so the mean scheduled number depended on exactly which days a participant reported. This matters because in the Nottingham studies a greater number of scheduled meals on a given day predicted greater energy intake that day (Farshchi et al., 2004 (Farshchi et al., , 2005)). We could not include the scheduled number of meals as a covariate, because we did not always know which day a recall referred to, but adding the reported number of meals as a covariate did not change the qualitative pattern of results. There was no evidence that the condition effects on free-living energy intake were driven by intake of any particular macronutrient.

The increase in ad libitum intake following the Informed-Irregular intervention parallels the objectively measured overeating reported in adults with FI provided with ad libitum food. In an inpatient study, food-insecure adults consumed more energy than food-secure adults over three days of unrestricted access to food from vending machines, both in absolute terms and relative to their weight-maintaining energy requirements, despite having eaten a weightmaintaining diet for the preceding five days (Stinson et al., 2018). The authors attributed this to a cycle of restriction when food is scarce and overeating when it becomes available, which is essentially the explanation that we offered, speculatively, for the opposite directions of our laboratory and free-living results. Evidence from women, in whom the association between FI and body weight is concentrated in high-income countries, is weaker. In a mock taste test conducted after a sugary preload intended to equalise cues of energetic need, opportunistic consumption of energy-dense snacks increased more steeply with current FI in women than in men, but only for one of two measures of FI, and the association with current FI was moderated by self-reported experience of FI in childhood (Nettle et al., 2019).

4.2.4 A threshold pattern

Wherever this pilot detected condition structure, it took the threshold form (Figure 9B): the Informed-Regular condition stood apart, while the three conditions involving irregularity, uncertainty or both behaved alike, and the Amplification model, which corresponds to our preregistered hypothesis, was never the best-supported. The pooled analysis of the three preregistered outcomes provides the most direct evidence for this pattern, because it rests on the outcomes that the study was designed to measure rather than on a subset of 29 largely exploratory outcomes. Taken together, DIT, GAD-7 and PHQ-9 distinguished the Informed-Regular condition from the other three conditions, in the direction of higher thermogenesis and fewer symptoms of anxiety and depression, which suggests that the metabolic and psychological outcomes may share a common response to any departure from a regular meal schedule known in advance rather than responding separately to irregularity or uncertainty.

Our factorial design separates two channels through which information about the future food supply might reach the systems that regulate energy storage: what a participant is explicitly told about her forthcoming meals (the Informed-Uncertain factor), and the variability that she actually experiences (the Regular-Irregular factor). This distinction between declarative and experienced information is rarely drawn in the FI literature, yet it matters for the insurance hypothesis, which is agnostic as to whether the perceived insecurity that drives fat storage is a reportable belief or an implicitly tracked property of the food supply (Nettle et al., 2017). Predictive-processing accounts of interoception and allostasis provide a plausible mechanism for the latter, whereby the organism generates predictions about energy availability and responds to prediction error irrespective of whether that error can be articulated (Peters et al., 2017). Two caveats apply. First, the Irregular condition delivers realised variance in the timing of meals rather than uncertainty per se; whether that variance is converted into an internal estimate of uncertainty is part of the hypothesis under test. Second, apart from a single retrospective item on worry about meal timing, we did not measure the internal states that the manipulations were intended to induce, such as how confident participants were about when their next meal would occur. We can therefore describe how outcomes responded to being informed or not and to regular or irregular meals, but not whether these manipulations produced two distinct states of uncertainty.

With those caveats, the observed pattern is informative. Rather than the two factors producing distinct signatures, the outcomes that showed any structure were most consistently differentiated by the contrast between the Informed-Regular condition and the other three. This is what would be expected if declarative and experienced information converge on a common internal estimate of when the next meal will occur, such that either irregular meals or the absence of advance information is sufficient to shift that estimate. It is notable in this context that the Uncertain-Regular schedule was, in principle, learnable: after a few days, participants could have inferred that their meals recurred at the same five times. If the tendency for this condition to group with the irregular conditions is confirmed, it would suggest that the absence of explicit information about future meals matters even when the experienced pattern of meals is regular. Not every outcome fitted the threshold pattern, however: worry about meal timing, the most direct subjective index of the manipulation, increased additively with uncertainty and irregularity. Moreover, the threshold interpretation was developed after inspecting the data, and across 29 outcomes a small number of apparently consistent effects could arise by chance. The pooled analysis is subject to the same caveat, because the contrast was chosen after inspecting the DIT data; moreover, with 12 participants its test of heterogeneity had little power, and GAD-7 on its own showed no detectable condition effect, so the pooled result may be carried mainly by DIT and PHQ-9. Given the size of this pilot, we therefore propose the threshold pattern as a hypothesis for an adequately powered confirmatory study rather than as a conclusion.

4.3. Limitations

The sample was small and comprised only healthy-weight, food-secure women, so the results may not generalise to other groups. The mixed-model estimates rest on few participants and correspondingly low denominator degrees of freedom, and the between-participant uncertainty manipulation involved only six participants per group, so the inferential results are best treated as indicative rather than definitive. Many outcomes were examined, most of them exploratory, and we did not correct for multiple comparisons.

4.4.

Recommendations for a full trial The pilot suggests several modifications for a full trial. First, engagement with the EMA app was borderline acceptable and declined over time, so engagement should be supported with monitoring, feedback and, potentially, incentives linked to engagement rather than to compliance (e.g. Neal et al., 2025). Second, the Irregular schedule should be redesigned to more closely reflect patterns of meal timing observed amongst individuals experiencing FI, by omitting meals from a fixed set of regularly spaced eating times, as in the Nottingham protocol, and varying the time of the first meal by omitting early meals on some days. Third, food should be provided, as in the two most recent Nottingham studies (Alhussain et al., 2016 (Alhussain et al., , 2022)), so that energy intake and diet composition are held constant across conditions. This would allow any effects to be unequivocally attributed to the temporal pattern of eating and uncertainty, rather than to the quantity or quality of food. Fourth, the internal states that the manipulations are presumed to induce, such as uncertainty about the timing of the next meal, should be measured directly, for example with EMA items measuring anticipated food scarcity (Folwarczny et al., 2021), so that the declarative and experienced routes can be distinguished empirically. Finally, if the threshold pattern is taken as the working hypothesis, a confirmatory study could compare the Informed-Regular condition with the single condition that combines irregularity and uncertainty (Uncertain-Irregular), concentrating power on the contrast that the pilot suggests is most informative rather than retaining the full 2 × 2 design. This would, however, sacrifice the ability to separate the effects of irregularity and uncertainty, so the choice of design should depend on whether the primary aim is to test the combined effect of irregularity and uncertainty on health or to separate their effects.

The rationale for further work is strengthened by a recent systematic review, in which between-day variability in meal pattern was associated with adverse outcomes, including higher body weight and a reduced thermogenic response to meals, in 24 of 34 papers; most of this evidence was cross-sectional, however, and the authors concluded that well-controlled intervention studies are needed to establish causation (Ali et al., 2024).

5. Conclusion

We have developed and piloted a protocol for experimentally manipulating the irregularity and uncertainty of meals in free-living adults. Part A showed that the protocol was feasible and acceptable, that it produced the intended changes in the timing of eating and that participants registered the uncertainty manipulation, although engagement with momentary assessment needs strengthening. In Part B, the pilot did not support our preregistered predictions, but it was not powered to provide strong tests of the hypotheses involving uncertainty, and equivalence tests indicated that the data cannot exclude meaningful effects. Exploratory analyses, including a pooled analysis of the three preregistered outcomes, suggested that, rather than uncertainty amplifying the effects of irregularity, any departure from a regular meal schedule known in advance may be sufficient to shift outcomes related to DIT, food intake and affective state. With the modifications described above, our protocol could be used in adequately powered trials to test whether meal irregularity and uncertainty impact markers of health and could contribute to the adverse effects of FI.

For logistical simplicity (and in common with the Nottingham protocol), for the Irregular schedule, we chose a single exemplar of a 14-day schedule created according to the above algorithm that we used for all participants (Supplementary Methods Table 2). There were two considerations in choosing this version of the schedule. First, days 1 and 2 were not overly harsh. The rationale for this was to break participants in gently and reduce the likelihood of drop out. Second, day 14 had five meals, with the final meal occurring at the same time as the final meal in the Regular condition. The rationale for this was to reduce the likelihood of laboratory results obtained the following morning (day 15) being dominated by acute effects of different periods of prior fasting (a similar approach was taken in the Nottingham protocol).

incorporates increased within-and between-day variability in the timing of meals of a similar magnitude to that seen in adults with FI in the USA and UK.

Table S22. Exploratory pooled test of the Informed-Regular vs other three contrast across the three preregistered outcomes (DIT, GAD-7, and PHQ-9).

Effect F df p Pooled contrast (Informed-Regular vs other three) 6.92 1, 62.90 .011* Outcome × Contrast (heterogeneity check) 0.46 2, 52.19 .632

Note. Each outcome's follow-up score was adjusted for its own baseline covariate and z-scored; GAD-7 and PHQ-9 z-scores were sign-flipped so that, on the combined scale, higher values consistently indicate the direction predicted for the Informed-Regular condition for all three outcomes (higher DIT; lower GAD-7/PHQ-9). The three harmonized z-scores were stacked and modelled jointly (outcome + contrast weight + random intercept for participant), with the contrast weight (+1 Informed-Regular, -1/3 each other cell) identical to the individual per-outcome contrasts. Because DIT was analysed via multiple imputation, the joint model was fitted separately within each of the 50 completed DIT datasets and pooled via Rubin's rules (GAD-7/PHQ-9 held fixed across fits), with Kenward-Roger degrees of freedom. The heterogeneity check tests whether the contrast differs across outcomes; a non-significant result supports treating the pooled estimate as a consistent effect rather than one driven by a single outcome. Significant p-values are shown in bold: * p < .050.

Schedule design

We designed a novel dietary intervention to manipulate meal irregularity (two levels: Regular versus Irregular) by manipulating the number and timing of meals scheduled each day. Irregularity was quantified with three variables: mean variance in the time intervals between meals within each day, variance in the time of the first meal each day, and variance in the number of meals each day (in all cases higher variance equates to more irregular). The manipulation of meal irregularity was based on the Nottingham protocol, but for increased ecological validity as a simulation of FI, we modified the meal schedules to more closely mimic the statistical features of the food-insecure diet extracted from 24-hour dietary recall data summarised in Supplementary Methods Table 1. In line with these data, we reduced the mean number of meals per day from 6 to 5 in both conditions. In the irregular condition, we increased the within-day variance in the time intervals between meals and introduced variation in the timing of the first meal each day. Details of the two conditions we produced are as follows.

The Regular condition always had exactly 5 meals per day, separated by 2.5-hour intervals. meals were scheduled to occur at the same times each day starting at 0800 hours. We chose 5 meals per day based on the US and UK datasets in which food-secure participants had means of 5.57 and 4.13 meals per day respectively. Our Regular condition reduced the mean within-day variability in the gaps between meals to zero and replicated the Nottingham protocol in having zero between-day variability in the number and temporal pattern of meals.

The Irregular condition had between 3 and 9 meals per day, drawn randomly without replacement from a distribution of 14 possibilities with a mean of 5 meals per day (3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9). The range of 3-9 meals was identical to that used in the Nottingham protocol's irregular condition, but we added positive skew by increasing the number of days with 3-4 meals and decreasing those with 7-9. Within each day, the meals were randomly scheduled to occur in any of the 26 possible 30-minute intervals between 08:00 and 21:00, with no constraints on the distribution allowed. This algorithm generated patterns of eating that had both within-day variability in the time intervals between meals as well as betweenday variability in the timing of the first meal of a day and the number of meals per day. The mean within-day SD in the time gap between meals of 103.56 minutes in our Irregular condition is comparable to the values of 118.7 and 98.0 minutes for participants with FI in the US and UK datasets respectively. Similarly, in our Irregular condition, the between-day SD in time of the first meal of 1.54 hours is comparable to the values of 1.42 and 1.56 hours for the US and UK datasets respectively. The SD in the number of meals per day in our Irregular condition of 1.96 is somewhat higher than the values of 1.10 and 0.76 for participants with FI in the US and UK datasets respectively, but is comparable to the value of 2.08 for the Irregular condition in the Nottingham protocol.

Figure 1.

Figure 1. Experimental design and lab-visit protocol. (A) Study design. The irregularity of meals was manipulated within participants (red and blue boxes) and uncertainty about the timing of meals between participants (white and grey boxes). Participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups and visited the lab four times, before (baseline) and after (follow-up) each 2-week intervention period. The two intervention periods were separated by a washout of approximately 2 weeks (minimum 13 days). (B) Timeline of each lab visit. Following arrival (weight and compliance questions) and 10 min supine rest, fasted expired gases were collected for 15 min, a fingertip blood sample was taken and the fasted appetite VAS was completed; completion of this VAS defined t = 0. A standardised breakfast was served at t = 15 min and consumed within 5-6 min. Appetite VAS were then completed every 30 min until t = 180 min, each followed immediately by a 15-min expired-gas collection. After the final gas collection, participants completed the CRAVE, Bond-Lader, POMS, PHQ-9 and GAD-7 questionnaires, followed by a battery of cognitive tests. The ad libitum test meal was served at t = 240 min. Hatched boxes indicate measures collected but not reported here. Timings before t = 0, and the durations of the questionnaires, cognitive tests and ad libitum meal, are approximate. CRAVE = Cravings for Rest and Volitional Energy Expenditure scale; GAD-7 = sevenitem Generalised Anxiety Disorder scale; PHQ-9 = nine-item Patient Health Questionnaire; POMS = Profile of Mood States; VAS = visual analogue scale.

Figure 9. Illustrative examples of the four patterns of condition means compared, ordered from simplest to most complex. (A) No effect: all four means are equal (0 additional parameters). Figure 10.

Figure 10. Contrast of the Informed-Regular condition against the other three conditions across the postprandial indirect-calorimetry outcomes. (A) Follow-up postprandial energy-expenditure timecourse; (B) diet-induced thermogenesis (net iAUC); (C) respiratory exchange ratio (RER), (D) fat oxidation and (E) carbohydrate oxidation across the postprandial period. Points and bars are modelpredicted means (EE and DIT pooled across imputations) +/-1 SE; faint lines in A are individual arm curves, black points in B are individual arms, and shaded bands in C-E are +/-1 SE.

Note.

Values are mean (SD). Energy-expenditure rows (resting EE, DIT) are pooled across 50 imputed datasets (Informed-Regular n = 6, Informed-Irregular n = 5, Uncertain-Regular n = 6, Uncertain-Irregular n = 6); substrate-oxidation rows are observed (non-imputed) values, for which cell sizes range from 4 to 6 sessions. Fasting = the fasted value at t = 0 min; postprandial = the mean of the t = 30-180 min values. DIT = diet-induced thermogenesis (net incremental area under the postprandial energy-expenditure curve above the t = 0 resting value, 0-180 min); RER = respiratory exchange ratio. a Preregistered outcome; all other variables were analysed on an exploratory basis.

Note.

Values are mean (SD); n = 6 per condition. Baseline = visit 1 (pre-intervention) and Follow-up = visit 2 (post-intervention) within each condition arm. GAD-7 = Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale; PHQ-9 = Patient Health Questionnaire 9-item scale; POMS = Profile of Mood States (total mood disturbance); Bond-Lader alertness/calmness/contentedness are visual analogue scale subscale scores (lower scores indicate greater alertness, calmness, and contentedness); CRAVE Rest and Move are motivation-state sub-scores (0-50).
